newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco stocks' real value unchained in settlement.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco stocks' real value unchained in settlement.

text.p: The $368.5 billion landmark settlement reached Friday between the tobacco industry, health advocates and 40 states suing the industry, will unlock years of suppressed value in tobacco shares, analysts say.
Tobacco stocks have suffered from the risk-averse nature of the stock market, and have the anaemic price-earnings ratios to show for it.
Under the current settlement plan, tobacco stock prices should begin to rise as the so-called "wall of worry" tumbles.
Investors will see the most critical outside threats to the earnings and dividends of tobacco stocks removed from harm's way and begin to apply steadier multiples.
How much higher are tobacco stocks likely to rise? Analysts at most Wall Street brokerage firms have set price targets that are by and large in line with one another.

Philip Morris should rise to around $60 a share. RJR Nabisco, which is poised for a spinoff of its tobacco operations now that the threat of litigation no longer implicates the assets of its 80.5-percent owned Nabisco Holdings Corp., will likely rise to about $45.
The stock of UST Inc., the leader in domestic sales of smokeless tobacco, is expected to rise to around $40 a share.

"The discount that's been applied to these stocks' valuations should easily exceed the cost of any settlement and, for that matter, the cost of litigation going forward even if there (were) no settlement," according to Roy Burry, analyst at Oppenheimer & Co.

The "discount" that Burry refers to is the difference between the price-earnings ratio of tobacco stocks as compared with P/E ratios of similar investment, such as other consumer-products companies and the Standard & Poor's 500 Index.
Traders price their risk aversion into what they are willing to pay for a company's shares. Tobacco stocks go cheap.
But any rally in the shares may be short-lived, according to Sanford C. Bernstein's analyst, Gary Black.

Black, in a research report issued late Thursday, said the stocks were likely to be hit by profit taking and return to some measure of volatility as the settlement attracts critics on its way to Capitol Hill, where it could face more trouble.

Meanwhile, Philip Morris Cos. Inc. -- one the strongest consumer-products companies in the world -- trades at about 17 to 18 times yearly earnings per share. RJR Nabisco Holdings moves at a P/E of 19. These are paltry numbers, given the cash flow on their balance sheets, analysts say.
In comparison, Coca-Cola Co. trades at about 43 times earnings. Procter & Gamble has a P/E ratio of almost 30, as does General Electric.
"The reason Coca-Cola trades at 43 times earnings and Philip Morris trades at 17 times earnings is that no one fears Coke kills people," said an asset manager who declined to be identified.
"Philip Morris is one of the best consumer-products companies in the world for growth, for return on the invested dollar (and) the growth of dividends.

"Why can you buy that kind of growth for a multiple that's just ridiculous? Because people -- for 25 years now -- have been afraid that that big cash flow ... water spout is being turned off, and that it is being turned off by forces outside the control of the company," he said.
Tobacco stocks rallied when the news first broke that settlement negotiations were underway. Has the benefit of a settlement been priced into share prices already?
"Very little," Burry said, adding that the Philip Morris stock has gained about $5 or $6 per share since the first signs of a settlement arose.
